text: Nvidia is now the world’s most valuable company, driven by the rise of artificial intelligence. At its core is the GPU — the Graphics Processing Unit, which Nvidia invented 25 years ago. In this article, I’ll explain why GPUs are the perfect chips for AI and how they propelled Nvidia to the top.
Here’s an outline of the article:

items: First, I’ll explain what a GPU is and how it differs from its cousin, the more familiar CPU

Then, I’ll cover the 3 waves of GPU adoption over the past two decades, focusing on why GPUs were the ideal chip for the last two: Wave 1: Video graphics in gaming. Wave 2: Cryptocurrency mining. Wave 3: Machine learning and AI

text: [1] What is a GPU?

A GPU, or Graphics Processing Unit, is a specialized semiconductor chip. A chip is made of many logic gates. If you’ve used Excel functions such as AND() or OR(), you already know the basic idea. For instance, the AND() function in excel takes two logical inputs (whose answer can be either “TRUE” or “FALSE”) and outputs “TRUE” only if both the 2 inputs are “TRUE”. Similarly an AND gate in a chip takes 2 inputs (in the case of semiconductor chips, these inputs are voltage signals) and outputs a signal only if both of them are “ON” or have a non zero voltage.

Logic gates are built from transistors — tiny switches that control the flow of electricity. Made from silicon, transistors allow current to pass under certain conditions. Modern chips contain trillions of transistors organized into billions of logic gates.
A GPU is a chip in which these transistors and logic gates are organized in a way to achieve some specialized functions.
[2] CPU vs. GPU

CPUs (Central Processing Units) and GPUs (Graphics Processing Units) are both semiconductor chips built to perform mathematical calculations, but they differ in architecture and purpose. They are not the only kind of semiconductor chips—memory chips, such as DRAM (which makes up a computer’s memory) or solid-state storage (“hard drive” of a computer) are also semiconductor chips.
Key Differences Between CPUs and GPUs

(a) Core count: CPUs and GPUs are built from cores — independent units in a processor (either CPU or GPU) that can process tasks independently. Complex tasks can be split into smaller parts and run across multiple cores in parallel, speeding up computation.
CPUs usually have far fewer cores than GPUs. For example, Apple’s M4 CPU has 10 cores, while Nvidia’s GeForce RTX 5090 GPU has over 20,000.

This difference gives GPUs a huge advantage in tasks that are “parallel” i.e. tasks that can be broken into 1000s of mini-tasks that are not dependent on each other. CPUs with a few cores are great for sequential tasks i.e. tasks where a step is dependent on the output from previous steps.

(b) Clock speed: Clock speed measures how fast a processor core can execute instructions. It is measured in gigahertz (GHz). A 1 GHz CPU can handle 1 billion instructions per second. For example, adding two numbers might require multiple instructions (like fetch number 1 from memory, fetch number 2 from memory etc). Therefore, a 1GHz CPU core can perform millions of additions per second.
CPUs generally run at higher clock speeds than GPUs. For example, Apple’s M4 CPU reaches 4.5 GHz, while Nvidia’s GeForce RTX GPUs run around 2 GHz.

There’s a tradeoff between having more cores and higher clock speeds. More cores generate more heat, especially if each core runs at a high clock speed. GPUs, with thousands of cores, have lower clock speeds to avoid excessive heat and power consumption. A CPU or GPU is typically part of a computer (laptop, servers etc) and, therefore, heat/power requirement is an important consideration.

In summary, GPUs are a type of semiconductor chip that has 1000s of cores. GPUs excel at tasks that require parallel processing. Use cases like video graphics, bitcoin mining and AI involve operations with parallel processing.
[3] GPU usage in Bitcoin mining:
GPUs were used for Bitcoin mining in the mid-2010s. Today, miners rely on ASICs (Application-Specific Integrated Circuits) — chips designed solely for Bitcoin mining.
How does Bitcoin mining works? A miner takes a block (collection) of transactions and a nonce (just a number) and then computes SHA256 hash of the combination.

A hash function transforms an input into a unique, fixed-size output. SHA256 is a popular hash function. Each input has a unique mapping, meaning a different input will always generate a different output. A small change in the input will produce a completely different output. The following table shows the SHA256 output for some inputs. Notice how the outputs change drastically for seemingly a simple change in input.

Miners cycle through millions of nonce values, each producing a different hash. The goal is to find one that meets a strict condition: the hash must begin with a certain number of leading zeros (e.g., “00000000ABCDEF…”). This condition is set by the Bitcoin protocol. The miner who is the first to submit a hash with the required number of leading zeros earns the Bitcoin mining reward, which is 3.25BTC at the time of writing.

This difficulty adjusts automatically as more miners join, ensuring that one block is mined about every 10 minutes. For instance, if there are many active miners then the Bitcoin protocol will require more leading zeros in the hash. Probability of generating a hash with more leading zeros is smaller and, therefore, miners have to try more combinations (i.e. guesses of nonces) to generate such a hash.
These characteristics make bitcoin mining a good use case for GPUs. Specifically:

items: Calculating hashes by varying nonces is a highly parallel operation. Each nonce can be processed independently. For example, a miner doesn’t need to complete hashes for nonces 1–100 before trying nonces 1000–1100, since hash functions have no correlation between inputs and outputs.
Billions of hashes must be computed to find one that meets the leading-zero requirement.

text: Professional mining rigs in 2025 can mine at rates exceeding 100 TH/s—calculating 100 trillion hashes per second.
[4] GPU usage in ML & Artificial Intelligence:

The goal is to create a model (which we can think of as a mathematical equation) that has analyzed billions of data points (called the training data) and encodes the patterns or "signal" in those data points in the model/mathematical equation. When presented with a completely new data point, the model uses what it learned from the training data to predict a response.

This is why GPUs are ideal for training ML and AI models—they excel at performing parallel operations, making them highly efficient for matrix computations at massive scales. Key takeaways:

items: GPUs are a type of semiconductor chip.

Compared to CPUs, they differ in two key ways: GPUs have thousands of cores, each acting as an independent processing unit within the chip. GPUs have lower clock speeds, meaning they are generally slower than CPUs for sequential tasks.
GPUs are ideal for use cases that require parallel processing, where tasks can be broken down into millions of smaller, independent operations that run simultaneously.
Examples of parallel processing applications include 3D game graphics, Bitcoin mining, and machine learning (ML) or artificial intelligence (AI) model training.
Bitcoin mining involves guessing hashes that meet specific requirements. Each guess is independent of the others, making it possible to distribute the workload across the thousands of cores in a GPU.

While GPUs were popular for Bitcoin mining in the mid-2010s, they are no longer profitable due to the rise of application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs), which are purpose built and optimized for calculating hashes

Training ML and AI models involves performing large-scale matrix multiplications. This requires billions of multiplication and addition operations that can be processed independently. Because of their parallel processing capabilities, GPUs are the ideal choice for this type of computation.
